The Miracle Beneath Our Feet: The Living Ground

What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and brings forth, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty. (Matthew 13:23)
Brothers and sisters, today we're going to talk about a very "down-to-earth" topic. And I mean that literally, because what we're talking about is the earth itself.

We often say someone has their "feet on solid ground," as if the ground were the most stable, unmoving thing there is. And when we call someone "earthy" or "plain as dirt," we mean they're about as unremarkable as can be.

But today I want to tell you two things. First, the ground is actually moving all the time. Second, that pinch of soil beneath your feet is a bustling city. From the tectonic plates deep below to the soil beneath our feet, the earth is always moving and always nurturing life.
As for the earth, out of it comes bread. Underneath it is turned up as it were by fire. Sapphires come from its rocks. It has dust of gold. (Job 28:5–6)
Earth's outer shell isn't one solid crust. It's divided into many plates, like a giant jigsaw puzzle, and these plates are slowly moving.
What's more, Earth is the only planet currently known to have active plate tectonics. Not one of our neighbors is as "alive" as Earth.

Plate movement builds mountains and forms mineral deposits. Job says, "Sapphires come from its rocks. It has dust of gold." The treasures deep in the earth are formed through exactly this kind of upheaval.

So the next time you see a gemstone sparkling, remember that its beauty was formed deep in the earth through a long process of being turned over. God's treasures are often formed under pressure and upheaval.
Plate tectonics has another function that few people know about. It carries carbonates from the seafloor back into Earth's interior, where volcanoes later release them as carbon dioxide.
This process has a long name: the "carbonate–silicate cycle." You don't need to remember the name; just remember what it does. It works like a long-term thermostat.

How does it work? When Earth warms up, rock weathering speeds up and absorbs more carbon dioxide, so the temperature comes down. When Earth cools, weathering slows down, and the temperature gradually rises again.

It's like the thermostat on an air conditioner. When it's too hot, it cools harder; when it's too cold, it eases off, keeping the room comfortable. Only Earth's air conditioner doesn't adjust over a few minutes; it works over very, very long stretches of time. Its strength and time scale are still being studied, but its role in stabilizing Earth's long-term temperature is already clear.
We think the ground is dead, but it's alive. We think it's still, but it's working all the time. In the world God made, even the rocks take part in His plan to sustain life.

This reminds me that God's work in our lives is the same. On the surface it may look like nothing has changed, but deep down He has been turning things over, adjusting and preparing all along. One day you'll see mountains raised up and treasures brought to light.

Are you going through a season of "upheaval" right now? A job change, a move, relationships shifting, as if your whole life has been turned upside down. Don't be afraid. The earth's upheaval raises mountains and brings out treasures, and God's upheaval in your life also comes with His good purpose.
2. A City of Life Beneath Our Feet
Let's bring the camera back up from deep underground to the surface. Imagine scooping up a small pinch of soil from the garden and holding it in your palm.
Do you know how many "residents" are in your hand? A small pinch of healthy soil is home to hundreds of millions of microbes, more than the number of people on earth.
What you're holding isn't a handful of mud. It's a megacity.

If these microbes had their own news channel, there would probably be big stories every day: the fallen leaves on such-and-such street have finished decomposing, nutrients have been delivered to such-and-such neighborhood, the roots of a certain plant have grown a little longer. We just can't hear it or see it.

The next time your kids come home covered in mud from playing outside, parents, don't rush to scold them. You might say, "Did you know there's a whole city in your hands?" Who knows, a little scientist and worshiper might be inspired that way.
What are these microbes doing? Quietly they break down fallen leaves and return nutrients to the plants.

In autumn the leaves cover the ground. Without these microbes, the leaves would pile up higher and higher, and forests would be buried under their own leaves. But because of this invisible cleanup crew, fallen leaves become nutrients, and the nutrients grow new leaves. Year after year, the cycle never stops.

This cleanup crew has another trait: they never pick and choose their work. Fallen leaves or dead branches, they take it all and turn it into nutrients. God often takes the "fallen leaves" of our lives too, our failures, tears and regrets, and turns them into nourishment for next season's growth.

So soil isn't just dirt and sand. It's a living system made of rock fragments, organic matter, water, air and countless living things. A single gram of soil may hold thousands of different kinds of microbes.

What's more, the vast majority of soil microbial diversity has not yet been named or studied, and it has been called one of biology's "final frontiers." Humanity can send probes into distant space, yet we still haven't figured out the soil beneath our own feet. That thought alone is humbling.
The earth's regulating and life-nurturing functions display a God who makes the land bring forth its produce and provides for every living thing.
You visit the earth, and water it. You greatly enrich it. (Psalm 65:9)
"You greatly enrich it." That richness doesn't come by itself. It's the result of God's care. He didn't just make the earth; He cares for the earth every day.
God often uses people no one sees
No one sees the microbes in the soil, yet they feed the whole earth. God, too, often uses unseen people and unseen things to accomplish great things.

It's the same in the church. Everyone can see the person preaching on stage, but someone came early to unlock the doors and set up the chairs; someone is quietly washing dishes in the kitchen; someone prays for the church at home every day. These people are like the microbes in the soil. There's no applause, but they bring the whole church to life.
If you are someone who serves quietly like this, I want to tell you today: your Father in heaven sees.

Sometimes people who serve quietly feel overlooked: "I've done so much, and nobody seems to notice." But think about the microbes in the soil. The whole forest owes its lushness to them, yet the forest has never put up a monument in their honor.
They don't need a monument, because their work itself is already a testimony to sustaining life. Your service is the same. In God's eyes, not one bit of it is wasted.
The focus is on the soil

Interestingly, when Jesus told the parable of the sower, the focus wasn't the seed, but the soil. The same seed, sown on the roadside, the rocky ground, among the thorns and on good soil, produced completely different results.

What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and brings forth, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty. (Matthew 13:23)
The seed is the same: God's word. The difference is the soil, which is our heart.

The roadside heart is as hard as a well-trodden path, and the word is snatched away as soon as it lands. The rocky-ground heart is enthusiastic at first, but its roots don't go deep. The thorny heart is crowded out by worries and all kinds of entanglements. Only good soil lets the word take root, grow and bear fruit.

We can also ask ourselves: what kind of heart did I bring to hear the word today? A heart that's thinking about my phone while I listen, a heart that only wants to hear an entertaining story, or a heart that's willing to be changed? The same message falling on different hearts produces different results.
Good soil can be broken up
The good news is that soil can change. Farmers plow the ground, pick out the stones and pull up the thorns. Our hearts can be broken up by God too.
Today, honestly ask yourself: is my heart like the roadside, the rocky ground, the thorns, or the good soil? Whatever the answer, you can hand it over to the best Farmer there is.
First, humility: a humble heart is good soil
Here's a fascinating bit of word history. In English, "humility" and "humus," which means soil, come from the same root.

How fitting that is. A humble heart is good soil. 321 says "humility overcomes pride." A proud heart is like concrete: nothing can grow in it. A humble heart is like soft, loose soil: when God's word is sown there, it can take root and bear fruit.

Proud people often say, "I already know that." Humble people say, "Lord, teach me again." The first is like hard-packed ground; the second is like freshly turned soil. Guess which patch of ground will grow something?
Second, life first, then relationships, then ministry
Fruit grows out of good soil. We're often in a hurry for fruit: results in ministry, growth in numbers. But 321 reminds us: life first, then relationships, then ministry.
When our life is healthy, ministry naturally bears fruit. Rather than tying fruit onto the tree, it's better to tend the soil first.

It's like the impatient farmer who saw that his neighbor's field was growing faster, so he went and pulled each of his seedlings up a little to help them grow faster, and they all withered. Growth in life can't be rushed. It starts at the roots.
Like the microbes in the soil, don't seek to be seen; seek only to nourish others. In Matthew 6:4, Jesus says your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
In an age when everyone wants to be seen, those who are willing to serve quietly are the most precious good soil in God's kingdom.

Think about it: how many unseen hands are behind your being able to sit here peacefully and worship today? Someone cleaned, someone prepared, someone prayed. Maybe this week, you can become one of those hands.

This week, do one act of service that nobody knows about, seen only by your Father in heaven. Don't take a photo, don't post about it, and don't mention it in small group. Let it be a little secret between you and your heavenly Father.

Brothers and sisters, the earth is alive. The plates deep underground are moving, regulating Earth's temperature. In the soil beneath our feet, hundreds of millions of tiny workers are quietly at work, feeding the whole earth.

If you can, find a chance this week to go outside and touch the soil. That is a place where God is at work every day. And let's hand our hearts over to the God who cares for the earth. Let's pray together.

Lord, thank You for making the living earth. Thank You for turning the movements deep underground into a blessing, for letting unseen microbes feed the whole earth, and thank You for caring for this earth every day and greatly enriching it.

Break up the hard ground of my heart. Remove the stones and thorns, and make me good soil, so that Your word may bear a hundredfold fruit in me. Give me a humble heart, willing like the soil to serve quietly, seen only by You. In Jesus' name, Amen.

The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it. (Psalm 24:1)

Friends, imagine that one day a very wealthy friend is going abroad for six months. He hands you the keys to his mansion and says, "Please look after the house for me. Water the garden, feed the fish, and feel free to stay there."

What would you do? If you're a sensible person, you'd probably be very careful. You'd water the plants and feed the fish on schedule. You wouldn't sell off the furniture or knock down walls to remodel. Because you know this house isn't yours. It has been entrusted to you by someone else.

Brothers and sisters, today is the last message in our Earth Hall. We've traveled from Earth's distance from the Sun, to the moon, water, the shield, breathing, the water cycle and the living ground. Today we want to answer the most fundamental question of all: who does this earth actually belong to?
The Bible's answer is clear: the earth is Yahweh's.
1. The Earth Is Full of God's Riches
Most of them we haven't met yet
Let me start with an astonishing number. Scientists estimate that there may be about 8.7 million species of eukaryotic life on Earth, yet so far only about 1.2 million have been formally named.
In other words, most of the creatures God made, we have yet to meet.
It's like touring a museum. You walk around for hours until your feet ache, and then a staff member tells you, "You've only seen a small part. Most of the galleries haven't even opened yet."

Sometimes we think we already understand this world pretty well. A quick scroll on our phones and we can look anything up. But before God's creation, even the experts have to admit there's so much they've never seen. That's not meant to discourage us; it's meant to excite us. It's like reading a great book, getting several chapters in, and discovering there's still a thick stack of pages to go, every one of them written by the same Author.
Yahweh, how many are your works! In wisdom, you have made them all. The earth is full of your riches. (Psalm 104:24)

The psalmist back then had no idea there were 8.7 million species, yet he was already amazed at "how many" there were. If he were alive today and saw these numbers, he'd probably write an even longer psalm.
God is not a stingy Creator. He didn't make just enough kinds to get by. He made them in abundance, more than we can count. His abundance is itself a hymn of praise.
It also reminds us that there is still so much about God's world that humanity doesn't know. Before God's creation, our best posture is curiosity, humility and worship.

Think about it: every species that hasn't been named yet is already known by God. People don't even know what to call it, but God has long known where it lives, what it eats and how it spends its days.

And what about you? You may feel very small in this world, as if nobody truly knows you. But the God who knows every little creature knows you even better. He knows your name, and He knows every feeling in your heart.
Let's look at a familiar example. Bees pollinate flowers, and flowers feed the bees. Flowers need bees and bees need flowers; neither can do without the other.
Now look at forests and rivers. Forests hold the soil and water in place, and rivers nourish the forests. They're like two old friends looking after each other.
Every living thing in an ecosystem is connected to others. Lose one link, and the whole web is affected.
We can picture an ecosystem as a tightly woven net. Cut one thread and it seems like nothing; the net is still there. But cut too many, and the whole net falls apart.
If you've got an older relative at home who knits, you'll know that if a sweater gets a small hole and nobody fixes it, the small hole slowly becomes a big one, until the whole sleeve unravels.

Our families are the same. Dad holds back a considerate word, Mom has a little less patience, the kids skip a greeting. Each seems so small, but over time the family, like that sweater, slowly comes loose. On the other hand, every little act of love weaves the net tighter.

The world God made isn't a pile of spare parts. It's an interconnected whole. This also shows us that God's heart is all about "relationship." He made all things to depend on one another and help one another flourish.
The church is the same. Every person is a thread in the net. You might think it doesn't matter if you're missing, but when you're gone, the whole net loses some of its strength.

Sometimes we say, "I'll skip small group today. One less person won't make a difference." But in God's design, no thread is unnecessary. Your presence, a word of greeting, a single prayer, all make this net stronger.
So please don't underestimate your place in God's family. You've been woven into this net, and God wove you in with His own hands.
In this great web, humans have a very special place. Human beings are the only creatures able to study, understand and consciously care for the whole earth.

That is a great ability, and a great responsibility. We can destroy, and we can also restore. Remember what we talked about in "The Invisible Shield"? The worldwide effort to repair the ozone layer is one example.
Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it. (Genesis 2:15)
The Bible gives humanity the role not of owner, but of steward. The earth belongs to God, we are entrusted to manage it, and one day we will give an account to Him.
Just like the story at the beginning, the keys are in our hands, but the house isn't ours. God placing the world into human hands is an act of trust in us, and also a calling for us.

Let me ask you a question: if God knocked on your door today and said, "I've come to see how the things I entrusted to you are doing," would you gladly open the door, or would you first say, "Hang on, let me tidy up a bit"? This question isn't meant to scare us, but to help us honestly see whether we're living with an owner's mindset or a steward's mindset.
You might ask, "The earth is so big. What can one person like me do?" Don't worry. God isn't asking you to carry the whole earth on your own. He Himself is caring for it.
See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns. Your heavenly Father feeds them. Aren’t you of much more value than they? (Matthew 6:26)
Look at a tree, a bird or a flower near you. They all belong to God, and God cares for them. And you are worth far more than they are.
So we serve as stewards not out of anxiety, but out of being loved. A steward who knows the master loves him will joyfully look after the master's house.

Let's go back to the story at the beginning. What if that friend didn't just hand you the house, but also said, "Help yourself to anything in the fridge. While I'm gone, treat it as your own home"? Wouldn't you take even better care of that house? Of course, because what you'd feel is trust and love. That's exactly how God treats us.
For the creation waits with eager expectation for the children of God to be revealed. (Romans 8:19)
What an amazing verse. All creation is waiting for God's children to be revealed.
When we live out the life of Christ, even the earth benefits along with us. A person truly changed by God treats the people around them differently, and treats the world God made differently too.

Think about it: what do your friends see in how you live? Do they see someone driven along by anxiety, or someone who knows "the earth is Yahweh's," and so has peace in their heart and open hands ready to give?
The earth is Yahweh's, and everything I have is His too. My time, money, body, family, and this earth have all been entrusted to me by God to manage.
Letting Jesus reign means changing "mine" into "His." When we see things this way, the way we spend money, use our time and treat our families will all be different.

Here's a simple example. When the paycheck comes in at the end of the month, an owner's mindset asks, "How am I going to spend this money?" A steward's mindset asks, "Lord, how do You want me to use this money?" The question differs by only a few words, but the direction of a whole life changes.
321 has a purpose: to build God's kingdom system. That sounds big, but it can start in very small places.

Within whatever I am responsible for, govern according to God's heart, so that His will is done on earth. If you manage a household, manage it according to God's heart. If you manage a department, lead it according to God's heart. That is building God's kingdom system right where you are.

You might say, "I'm not a manager. I'm not in charge of anything." But everyone has their own sphere: your desk, your phone, the words you speak, a weekend of your time. Letting God be Lord of even these small places is already building God's kingdom system.
Third, people matter more than things
We manage creation to bless people, not to possess things. We care for the environment so that people can live better; we manage resources so that more people can be blessed.
If we hurt people for the sake of getting things done, we've got it backwards. In God's eyes, people matter more than things.

For example, in a very tidy home, if a parent yells at the kids every day over a bit of dust on the floor, the house may be clean, but the children's hearts get hurt. A good steward manages things, but treasures people. That's God's perspective.

This week, choose one concrete way to care for creation, such as cutting down on waste or picking up litter, and invite a friend to do it with you. As you do it, talk with them about why you believe the earth is Yahweh's.
You'll find that when you bend down to pick up a plastic bag, you're actually saying to God, "Lord, I remember that this is Your earth." Small things like that are a form of worship too.
Brothers and sisters, congratulations! Together we've completed the Earth Hall!

From a distance that's just right, to the moon that steadies the earth; from wonderful water to the invisible shield; from the breathing earth, the journey of water and the living ground, all the way to today's earth entrusted to us. We have seen a God who prepared a home for us and watches over it day and night.
This God has handed us the keys. One day, when we give our account to Him, may each of us hear Him say, "Well done, good and faithful servant." Let's pray together.
Lord of all, everything is Yours. The earth and its fullness, the world and those who dwell in it, all belong to You. Thank You for making such a rich world, and thank You for entrusting it to us.

Make me a faithful steward who takes good care of all You have entrusted to me: my time, money, body, family, and this earth. Help me build God's kingdom system within whatever I am responsible for, so that Your will is done on earth. And one day, may You say to me, "Well done, good and faithful servant." Plates and Volcanoes: When the Ground Beneath Your Feet Is Walking Too
For the mountains may depart, and the hills be removed, but my loving kindness will not depart from you, and my covenant of peace will not be removed,”says Yahweh who has mercy on you. (Isaiah 54:10)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! First, please look down at your fingernails. Do you see them? Your nails are always growing and you never feel it, until one day you tap on your phone and hear that clicking and remember it is time to trim them.

Today I want to tell you something a little unbelievable: the ground under your feet is walking at about this speed. I did not make up that line; it is a comparison from the United States Geological Survey. You are sitting on a chair in church, the chair is on the floor, the floor is on the foundation, the foundation is on an enormous slab of rock, and that slab is moving. You did not buy a ticket, and you are on board all the same.

Here is another picture. Mount Everest, the highest in the world. Climbers spend a fortune and risk their lives to reach the top, and what is the rock under their feet? Fossil-bearing marine limestone, an ancient sea bed. You struggle to the top of the world and find yourself standing on the bottom of the sea. God’s sense of humor is sometimes very big.

Today we walk into the Earth Hall to look at this moving crust. We will see a piece of the history of science, see a precise working of the earth, and also ask honestly: if the ground moves, what should our lives stand on?
1. An idea that waited half a century

In 1912 there was a 32-year-old German named Wegener. His specialty was meteorology, but he came forward with a claim that made geologists frown: the continents were once joined together and later drifted apart. It was as if a dentist today went to an aerospace conference to present a rocket design. You can imagine the faces.

His difficulty was real: you say the continents drift, so what force pushes them? How could such enormous blocks of rock move? He could not answer. The opposition of the scientific community at the time had its reasons; science is supposed to ask about mechanism. In 1930 Wegener died on an expedition across the Greenland ice sheet. To the end of his life he never saw his idea accepted.
Brothers and sisters, sometimes you do something right and never live to hear the applause. Keep that sentence in your heart for now, because we will come back to it.

The turning point came at sea. During the Second World War there was a Princeton geologist named Hess serving in the US Navy as captain of a transport ship. Others fighting a war were just fighting a war, but on the voyage to the next battle this captain had his crew run echo soundings and measure the shape of the seafloor on the side. That is an occupational habit, and a blessed one.

In 1962 Hess published “History of Ocean Basins,” arguing that new seafloor is created at mid-ocean ridges and pushed out to both sides. The next year, 1963, two British scholars, Vine and Matthews, found that the magnetic stripes in seafloor rock are symmetrical on both sides of the mid-ocean ridge.

Let me give you a picture. The seafloor is like a tape slowly being fed out from the middle. When magma cools, the magnetic minerals in it record the direction of the Earth’s field at that time. Each time the field reverses, the next stretch is recorded in the opposite direction. Humanity rewound the tape, listened, and heard the history of the seafloor.
From 1912 to 1963 is a full half century. The idea that no one accepted back then returned in a more complete form.
Spiritual meaning: the lesson of waiting

Psalm 104 has a line: “The mountains rose, the valleys sank down, to the place which you had assigned to them.” This is a poem, and we do not use it as a geology textbook; its point is praise. But as I stand before this history, I see one thing: God’s works are counted in tens of millions of years, human discoveries in decades, and we often cannot wait even three weeks.
How long have you prayed for your child? How long have you waited, holding to honesty at work? Your fingernails grow every day, you just do not see it. God’s work in you is the same.
The mountains rose, the valleys sank down, to the place which you had assigned to them. (Psalm 104:8)
2. The island of Taiwan was made by a collision
A slow-motion car crash, eight centimeters a year

For our Chinese-speaking friends this topic hits especially close. The Central Weather Administration often uses this number to explain earthquakes in Taiwan: the Philippine Sea Plate pushes toward Taiwan at about 8 centimeters a year. Scholars have used GPS to measure Lanyu moving relative to Penghu at about 81.5 millimeters per year.

How much is 8 centimeters? About the width of a hand. You would not notice it in a year, but imagine two cars colliding at that speed and pressing together for a very, very long time. What happens to the hood? It crumples. You can think of the Central Mountain Range as the Earth’s crumpled hood.

Researchers say Taiwan is the product of the Luzon volcanic arc colliding with the margin of continental China, a collision that is still going on, with the Huatung Valley as the seam. So when you visit Hualien and take a photo standing in the middle of the valley, strictly speaking your left foot and right foot are standing on the two sides of a collision that is not over.
Brothers and sisters in other places, your story under your feet is a little different, but we all live on the same moving planet.

The moving crust has another role. In 1981 three scholars, Walker, Hays and Kasting, proposed that Earth has a feedback system that regulates temperature over the long term. Let me use the household account book. Volcanoes breathe carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere, which is a deposit. Rock weathering carries carbon dioxide away and finally turns it into carbonate that settles on the seafloor, which is a withdrawal.

The wonderful thing is this: the hotter the weather, the faster the weathering, the faster the withdrawals, and the less greenhouse gas; the colder the weather, the slower the weathering, and the withdrawals slow down too. Some of the carbonate that sinks to the seafloor is carried down with the plates, and comes back to the atmosphere through volcanoes.
Venus next door is very different: a surface of about 465 degrees Celsius, a pressure more than ninety times Earth’s, and no global plate network.
Spiritual meaning: honesty matters more than looking impressive
At this point many speakers add: “See! No plates, no life, so God must exist!” Brothers and sisters, I have to put on the brakes here.

The very scholars who proposed the thermostat mechanism said themselves that the numerical details are speculation and that the mechanism is only a partial stabilizer. Recent model studies also find that planets without plate motion could, under certain conditions, stay habitable. Whether Venus once had oceans is still unsettled. We have only one sample in hand, the Earth.

So I will not tell you that science has proved God. What I will tell you is that when I see this working, the line from the Psalms wells up in my heart: “Yahweh, how many are your works! In wisdom, you have made them all.” That is the eye of worship, an interpretation of faith. If a friend does not see it that way, we respect him. Christians are set free by the truth, and we do not need to exaggerate on God’s behalf.
3. The ground moves; where shall I stand?
Does “should not be moved forever” fight with GPS?

An inquirer asked me: Pastor, Psalm 104 says plainly that God “laid the foundations of the earth, that it should not be moved forever,” yet geology says the earth is always moving. Is the Bible wrong?

It is a good question. In the same psalm it also says God covered the earth with the deep “as with a cloak.” You would not ask what fabric that cloak is made of. This is the language of poetry, and what it conveys is that the earth holds up our lives securely, and what holds it up is God. When the weather anchor says the sun sets today, nobody reports him for violating astronomy.
The Bible itself knows that mountains move. Isaiah says it frankly: “the mountains may depart, and the hills be removed.” And then he turns and points to what truly does not move.
For the mountains may depart, and the hills be removed, but my loving kindness will not depart from you, and my covenant of peace will not be removed,”says Yahweh who has mercy on you. (Isaiah 54:10)

The Gospel of Matthew records two earthquakes. The first came when Jesus breathed His last: “The earth quaked and the rocks were split.” The second came on the morning of the resurrection: “Behold, there was a great earthquake.” I want to invite you to notice this picture. On the darkest afternoon and the brightest morning in human history, the earth responded.

This same Jesus told a parable about two houses. Rain came down, floods came, winds blew; one house fell and one did not, and the difference was the foundation. People who live in an earthquake zone understand this parable best: a beautiful house is no use, what counts is the structure and the foundation.

“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock. (Matthew 7:24-25)
Spiritual meaning: the kingdom that cannot be shaken

Our sense of security is often built on things that move. Work moves, health moves, children grow up and leave home, savings shrink, and the person we thought would never change has changed. Only then do we discover that we had been living on a plate all along.

Hebrews tells us that what Jesus brings us is a kingdom that cannot be shaken. He went to the cross and bore our sin; He rose from the dead and opened the way. God’s loving kindness does not stay only if I perform well today; what He established is a covenant.

This is the practical meaning of “let Jesus reign”: moving the foundation of life from human, temporary things to God’s eternal promise. It is no longer me holding everything up; it is Christ holding me.

Brothers and sisters, please take three things home. First, the Bible is my standard. Choose one word of the Lord and really do it this week; that is laying a foundation. Second, letting God be God and people be people. People can measure how many centimeters a plate moves each year, but cannot stop it by even one centimeter; admitting our limits is the beginning of wisdom. Third, people matter more than tasks.

This week there is a very concrete action: spend fifteen minutes with your family checking the emergency go-bag and agree on a meeting point after an earthquake. Then check in on an older person who lives alone and see whether the cabinets in their home need securing. Faith and earthquake preparedness do not conflict. Those who trust God should be all the more careful to build their houses well and look after their neighbors.
If you want to talk with a friend, you can ask lightly: in your life, what is there that could not be shaken away even if heaven and earth shook? No need to hurry him to answer. Just listen.

Let us be quiet, look at our fingernails once more, and think about the ground moving under our feet and the Lord who has never dozed off. Lord who laid the foundations of the earth, my life often shakes and I am often afraid. Thank You that Your loving kindness does not depart from me, and thank You that Jesus has opened to me the kingdom that cannot be shaken. Rebuild my life on Your words. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Wegener never saw his idea accepted. Is there something right in your life that you have done for a long time without yet seeing its fruit? How do you face the waiting?

2. We talked about not exaggerating on God’s behalf, for example not saying “science has proved God.” Why does this kind of honesty actually help in sharing the gospel? Have you met the opposite example?
3. What are you building your sense of security on right now? What would happen if that ground moved? Which word of the Lord do you want to act on this week?
The Deep Sea: A Wonder No One Sees
“Have you entered into the springs of the sea? Or have you walked in the recesses of the deep? (Job 38:16)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! First, think of a book. This book has a hundred thousand pages, so thick that your bookshelf at home cannot hold it and you would need a whole warehouse. Humanity has spent seventy years reading this book. How much have we read? Less than one page. And that page was not turned evenly; most of the turning was in the same few paragraphs of the same chapter. And then we stand up and say: I roughly know what this book is about.

This book is called the deep sea. In 2025 Dr. Bell’s team added up, record by record, the publicly available deep-sea dive records from around the world, about forty-four thousand dives, and calculated that the deep seafloor humans have seen with their own eyes or with cameras is less than 0.001 percent. How big is that in area? About one tenth of Belgium. The largest habitat on the whole Earth, and we have seen only this small a piece of it.
When Job was in his deepest pain and most wanted answers, God asked him a question. In three thousand years this question has not expired, and it works just as well on us today.
“Have you entered into the springs of the sea? Or have you walked in the recesses of the deep? (Job 38:16)

Today I want to take you on three dives. On the first, we see how much people know. On the second, we see what really lives in that darkness. On the third, we ask a question that has a lot to do with your Monday morning: does something that no one sees have any value?
1. A book of a hundred thousand pages, and we have read less than one
Let’s get the numbers straight first

We often hear the saying that humans have explored only five percent of the ocean. Brothers and sisters, this kind of number spreads widely, but ask “what does explored mean?” and nobody can answer. As Christians we should speak more honestly than internet rumors, so let me separate things.

The first number: according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration of the United States, as of April 2026 about 28.7 percent of the global seafloor has been mapped with modern high-resolution sonar. The second number is the one I gave you just now, less than 0.001 percent, and it refers to the seafloor below two hundred meters that someone has actually seen in images.

Sonar mapping is like drawing the street map of a city from an airplane: you know where the roads are, but not who lives inside. Seeing it with your own eyes is when you ring the doorbell, walk in, and sit down. We now have rough street sketches of about thirty percent, and the houses we have entered are pitifully few.

What is more interesting is that Bell’s study also found that more than sixty-five percent of the places we have looked at are concentrated near the United States, Japan and New Zealand, and nearly thirty percent of the records are low-resolution photos from before 1980. Brothers and sisters, it is as if an alien had seen only two exits of a Taipei MRT station and then written a paper about human beings.

The ocean covers more than seventy percent of the Earth’s surface, with an average depth of about 3,682 meters. The deepest point, Challenger Deep, is about 10,935 meters. Move the whole of Mount Everest into it, and the summit is still two kilometers below the surface, with room for ships to sail above. At that depth, for every ten meters or so you go down, the pressure goes up by about one atmosphere, so you can work out for yourself that it is over a thousand atmospheres.
Spiritual meaning: admitting we haven’t finished reading

Brothers and sisters, when God asked Job that question, He was not humiliating him. He was bringing Job to the right place: what you do not know is far more than what you know. This honesty is the beginning of humility. Let God be God and people be people. It is the same with our knowledge of God: what you and I have read is probably about that one page. So with brothers and sisters who see things differently, our tone can be a little gentler.
A boatload of people who brought no biologist

In February 1977, at the Galápagos Rift, out at sea several hundred kilometers from the coast of Ecuador, a group of geologists went looking for hydrothermal vents on the seafloor. The submersible Alvin carried the pilot Donnelly and two scientists, Corliss and van Andel, down to about twenty-five hundred meters. Everyone thought there would be nothing alive down there, so the whole expedition did not bring a single biologist.

After they descended, outside the window there appeared clams, mussels, crabs, octopuses, and tube worms wearing red crowns, packed densely together. The surrounding water was about two degrees Celsius, while beside the vents it was much warmer. These geologists hurriedly took samples, but they had not brought enough formaldehyde. What to do? They took out the Russian vodka they had bought in Panama and soaked the specimens in it. I do not know what that bottle was originally meant to celebrate, but in any case it made a contribution to science.

Why did this change biology? Because almost every food chain on land begins with the sun: grass eats sunlight, cows eat grass, we eat cows. Here the starting point was bacteria, using the hydrogen sulfide from the vents to make nutrients. That is the stuff that smells to us like rotten eggs. By 1981, Cavanaugh and colleagues reported in the journal Science that the cells inside the giant tube worms were very likely just this kind of symbiotic bacteria.

We can think of it this way: a whole city has a blackout and is pitch dark, yet one neighborhood is brightly lit, every household has its own little generator, and the fuel is something other people threw away because it stinks. God’s creation can use even the smell of rotten eggs.

Let us go up and down a bit further. Two scientists at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute went through 17 years of remotely operated vehicle footage, from the surface to about 3,900 meters, and classified the animals one by one, more than 350,000 of them. About seventy-six percent could produce their own light.

I must add something honestly: this is a statistic from off California, and we cannot yet say it is the same worldwide. Scientists also have good explanations for what the lights are for: some lure prey, some attract mates, some are for escaping. That world has eating and being eaten too, and it is not a picture of nothing but poetry. A friend who does not believe in God may say to you: all this is the result of natural selection, “beauty” is something you project onto it, and the deep sea does not care. On the mechanism there is a great deal of evidence for that view, and we should respect it.

What we want to add is another layer of question. The mechanism tells us how the light came about, but it does not tell us why this world is so abundant, far beyond what anyone needs. That is an inference of faith, not an experimental result, and we do not say that science has proved God. But the psalmist, standing by the shore long ago, said it this way:

LORD, how many are your works! In wisdom, you have made them all. The earth is full of your riches. There is the sea, great and wide, in which are innumerable living things, both small and large animals. (Psalm 104:24-25)
Spiritual meaning: abundance does not wait for approval

Genesis says God made the living creatures of the waters, and “God saw that it was good.” At that time there were no people on the earth. Brothers and sisters, there was only one judge on that scorecard. That little creature four thousand meters down that flashed once has never appeared in any video, and its existence was long ago called good.
3. The One who watches in secret

Now for our third dive, down into your own life. We live in an age of likes. You post a photo and every five minutes check how many people responded. It is the same with ministry: you set out the chairs and nobody knows, and your heart goes a little sour; you preach and nobody praises you, and you do not sleep well that night. I am the same. I am not talking about other people.

But think about how many of the things that really matter in your life happen in places without lights. Caring for a mother with dementia and answering the same question for the thousandth time. Praying late at night for someone who hurt you. Holding back the cruel thing you badly wanted to say. No one will film these things, and no one will give an award.
But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly. (Matthew 6:6)

Jesus said God is “your Father who is in secret.” That is where He usually is. You think that after that door is shut there is no one, but that is exactly where He is at work. This is what the 321 teaching calls selflessness: I no longer need to be seen in order to go on living, because the One I care about most has already seen. This also needs to be said to those suffering in the dark: your tears are not unknown. If you are being hurt in secret, please tell one person you trust. God wants you to receive help, and does not want you to carry it alone.
The One who went down to the deepest place

Finally, Jesus Himself linked the depths of the sea with His own death. Jonah prayed in the sea that God had thrown him into the deep and that the waves and billows passed over him. What did Jesus say?
For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the huge fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. (Matthew 12:40)

Notice the direction. Our Savior did not stand on the shore throwing a life ring. He went down Himself, down into death, down to the deepest place of being forsaken by God. And then on the third day He came up from there. So no matter how deep you have fallen today, there is no place there that He has not been.
Spiritual meaning: thrown where no one can fish it up

There is one more thing I especially like. The prophet Micah says that God will “cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.” Brothers and sisters, we just said that humans have not even seen one hundred-thousandth of it. That is where God throws your sins. Because of the cross, this word has been made good. Those things you keep wanting to dive down and fish up, to blame yourself one more time: please do not go down again. There are no submersible reservations there.

Brothers and sisters, the deep sea teaches us three things. First, honestly admit that we have not finished reading; this is humility. Second, God’s abundance does not wait for people’s approval. Third, the places no one sees are exactly where the Father who is in secret is. This week, please do one small thing: quietly do a good thing for someone, pay a bill, tidy a corner, write out a prayer, with no name attached, and do not give in to the urge to tell about it three days later. If you have a friend who does not yet believe, you can also ask him: if a good deed you did were never known by anyone, would it still have value in your opinion? Then listen quietly.

Let us pray together: Lord who made the deep sea, Your riches far exceed what I know. Thank You for watching in secret, and for seeing my tears and struggles that no one knows. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for going down to the depths of death for me and rising again. Let me keep shining faithfully in places without applause. In Jesus’ name, amen.

1. The picture of a hundred-thousand-page book of which we have read less than one: what new feeling does it give you about how well you know God? Is there anything about the faith that you have stated too confidently?
2. Is there something in your life that you feel less like doing because no one sees it? Is God’s “watching in secret” a comfort or a pressure to you? You can say so honestly.

3. Micah says God throws sins into the depths of the sea. Is there something you have already confessed that you still often dive down to fish up and blame yourself for? How can we remind one another?
Forests: The Earth’s Lungs and Network
Then all the trees of the woods shall sing for joy (Psalm 96:12)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Today I’m going to ask everyone to do something a little embarrassing: think back to your phone. When the Amazon burned in 2019, did you ever forward a line saying that the Amazon is the lungs of the Earth and produces twenty percent of the world’s oxygen? If you did, no need to raise your hand. We’ll let you keep a little dignity.

That year the big media said it, and the French president and a US senator posted it. But when the fact-checking websites asked the scientists, the answer was: that line is wrong. And not slightly wrong.

Today we come to the Forest Gallery of the Earth Hall. I am going to do something preachers don’t usually dare to do, which is to take apart two very handy sermon illustrations. One is “the lungs of the Earth,” and the other is the “wood wide web” that has become so popular in recent years. When we are finished, my hope is that you will have not less awe for the forest and for the Lord who made it, but more. Real things usually stand up to a close look better than exaggerated versions do.
1. The lungs of the Earth? A correction

Let’s do the accounts. Trees photosynthesize and give off oxygen; you learned that in middle school, and it is true. But trees also breathe, and at night especially they use oxygen. When leaves fall and trees topple, microbes decompose them and use up a big sum of oxygen again. Professor Malhi at Oxford has calculated that the Amazon’s gross production is about nine percent of the world’s oxygen, while another scholar, Foley, estimates about six percent. Subtract what it uses itself, and what is the net contribution? Malhi’s answer: almost zero.

Think of it like a buffet restaurant doing very good business. A lot of money comes in every day, but after the rent, the wages and the ingredients are paid, at the end of the month it just breaks even. How much has it added to the nation’s savings? About zero. But would you dare say the street would be just as well off without it?

So where does the oxygen we breathe come from? Mainly from an enormous stockpile accumulated over geological ages. Some geologists have calculated that even if all non-human life on Earth were burned up, the oxygen concentration would only fall from 20.9 percent to about 20.4. So you can sleep soundly tonight.
Incidentally, the lung is an organ that uses oxygen; it does not produce it. In a certain sense, the metaphor is right by accident.

So does that mean forests don’t matter? Please don’t hear it that way. The 2025 assessment of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization says the world’s forests cover about 4.14 billion hectares, thirty-two percent of the land, and hold about 714 gigatonnes of carbon. They are among the largest land-based carbon warehouses in the world, and once they burn, the carbon goes back into the air.

Forests also make rain. A 2012 study in Nature used satellite data from the tropics and found that if air first drifts over forest, the rainfall afterward rises markedly. Tree roots pull water up from the ground and it evaporates from the leaves, which is like opening a river in the sky. The Amazon is thought to be the key to stabilizing rainfall in South America, and one scientist has compared it to the planet’s giant air conditioner.

So the more accurate metaphor is this: the forest is the central air conditioning and water tower of the whole building. When it shuts down, you won’t suffocate right away, but the climate of the entire building will be thrown into chaos. As for deforestation, the good news is that it is slowing, from 17.6 million hectares a year in the 1990s to 10.9 million hectares a year in 2015 to 2025. The bad news is that this is still about three Taiwans every year.
Spiritual meaning: no need to embellish for God

Brothers and sisters, why am I spending so much time correcting one number? Because it is very easy for Christians to feel that when we are praising creation, a little exaggeration does no harm. That is wrong. The One who said “I am the truth” does not need us to pad His case. If you pass a false number to a friend today and he checks it tomorrow, he may stop believing the gospel you shared along with it. The Bible is my standard, and that includes the ninth commandment.
2. The wood wide web? Said too strongly

The second metaphor is even more beautiful. In 1997 the Canadian scholar Suzanne Simard and her colleagues published a study in Nature. They found in the field that carbon could be transferred, net, between different tree species through mycorrhizal fungi underground. The symbiosis of fungi and tree roots had long been known, but that something flows between one tree and another made people’s eyes light up.

Later the research was passed around and grew bigger and bigger, until it became a moving story: beneath the forest lies a network, mother trees recognize their children and send them nutrients and alarms, and a dying old tree even hands down an inheritance to the young ones. Friends, to a preacher, hearing this is like finding a pot of ready-made broth. Loving one another, spiritual parents, it is all there. I confess that I wanted to use it too.
The one who tapped the brakes was an original author

But in 2023, three scholars published a review in Nature Ecology and Evolution. One of them, Professor Jones, was a co-author of the 1997 paper. Friends, this is one of our own going back to check our own.

What did they find? First, only five studies had actually used genetic sequencing to confirm that trees and fungi form a network, and they involved two tree species, so “spread throughout the forest” cannot yet be said. Second, the results of 26 field studies each had other possible explanations: perhaps the roots were simply touching, perhaps the nutrients passed through the soil. Third, that mother trees give priority to their own offspring: they found no peer-reviewed field evidence for it at all.

What was more sobering was the part about citations. They traced how 18 key studies were cited and found that the later the paper, the more likely it was to say more than the original study. In the category about function, the citations not supported by the original studies came close to half. So even scientists pass around that “seems so moving” message.

To be fair, this does not mean Simard’s research is false. Mycorrhizal symbiosis is established fact, and carbon moving between seedlings has been seen in the laboratory. The network researchers still have good reason to keep exploring, and they led many people to look at the forest as a whole again, which is a contribution. It is only that current knowledge, as these three authors put it, is still too thin and too uncertain. In 2024 another group of plant scientists also warned that describing trees as mothers who look after their children carries considerable risk. The conclusion: we don’t know yet. “We don’t know yet” is a phrase well worth Christians learning to say.
Spiritual meaning: loving one another needs no endorsement from fungi

So what do we do when we talk about loving one another? Please notice that Jesus never said, love one another because the trees in the forest do it too. He said, as I have loved you. Our basis is Him, and we do not need to wait for fungi to vouch for it. If research someday finds that trees really do help one another, we can praise God together; if it doesn’t, the love on the cross is not one bit less.
Two verbs and a law of war

The Bible’s attitude to trees is actually quite interesting. God caused every tree to grow, “pleasant to the sight, and good for food.” Pleasant to look at comes first. He is a God who cares even about beauty. Then He placed the man there and gave him two verbs:
Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it. (Genesis 2:15)

Cultivate and keep. It is like a neighbor going abroad and handing you the keys. The flowers need watering, the doors need locking, and when he comes back you would be ashamed to hand over a wasteland. This does not mean we can’t use timber; the Israelites built houses too, and built the temple. It means we are stewards, not landlords.

What I like best is this line in Deuteronomy, where even in the middle of war God speaks up for the trees: when besieging a city you shall not destroy its trees with an ax, and “is the tree of the field man, that it should be besieged by you?” Ancient armies besieging a city often started by wrecking the enemy’s farms and orchards, so in that world this regulation is a truly surprising thing to say.
The heaviest tree in the Bible

Now pull the camera back. The first scene in the Bible has a tree of life, the last scene has one too, and in between stands the heaviest tree of all. When Peter wrote his letter, the word he used was “tree”:
He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness. You were healed by his wounds. (1 Peter 2:24)

Adam’s hand reached for the fruit on a tree, wanting to rule for himself; Christ’s hands were nailed to a tree, returning the sovereignty to the Father. The self-centered life began there, and selflessness is completed here. On the third day He rose again. So at the very end, in Revelation, we can see that the leaves of the tree of life are “for the healing of the nations.” The whole story of the Bible goes from one tree, past another tree, to yet another tree.
Spiritual meaning: all the trees of the woods shall sing for joy

The psalm says that when the Lord comes, “all the trees of the woods shall sing for joy before Yahweh.” This is poetry, not botany, and trees have no mouths. But it tells us that creation is waiting for something, and the forest is within that hope. So the small acts of keeping we do today are not in vain. Let Jesus receive all the glory, and that includes the tree in your yard.

Brothers and sisters, this week please do two small things. First, check one “seems so moving” message you once forwarded, and correct it if it was wrong. That is more Christian than forwarding a hundred more. Second, find a tree near your home, stand under it for three minutes, and find out its name. You can also ask a friend who does not yet believe: do you remember a tree from your childhood? What did it make you feel? Many conversations begin with a tree.

Let us pray together: Lord who made the trees, thank You for letting the forests regulate the climate and bring rain for me without my ever noticing. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for being hung on wood for me, and for rising again, and for giving me the hope of the tree of life. Help me to speak the truth, and to keep well the earth You have entrusted to us. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Have you ever believed or forwarded a “moving story” that you later found was not accurate? How did you react when you found out?
2. Can you say “we don’t know yet” in your life of faith? What effect do you think saying it to an unbelieving friend would have?
3. What is one concrete small thing you could do this week to put “cultivate and keep” into practice in your home and your neighborhood?
Natural Disasters: Sit Down First, Then Speak
Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit. (Psalm 34:18)
Brothers and sisters, peace to you. This sermon I am not going to open with a joke. I would like to ask everyone to be quiet for a moment.

September 21, 1999, 1:47 in the morning. Friends who were living in Taiwan then probably still remember where you were. That earthquake took 2,415 people, left 29 missing, and injured more than ten thousand. The South Asian tsunami of 2004: about 228,000 people. Türkiye and Syria in 2023: more than 55,000. I read these numbers aloud, but I know that for some people, numbers are not numbers. That is a father, a daughter, an old home that can never be returned to.

If you are that person today, I want to say to you first: I am sorry. You do not have to work anything out today. You can keep sitting, you can step outside for some air, and you can be angry with God. You will not be thrown out of this room for it. In this sermon I will not tell you “it was all for the best,” because I have no right to say that, and the Bible does not ask me to.
Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit. (Psalm 34:18)
Job’s friends got seven days right

Let’s look first at Job’s three friends. Many people criticize them, but at the beginning they did it right. The Bible says they saw Job from a distance and did not recognize him, so they wept aloud and threw dust on their heads. And then?
So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great. (Job 2:13)

Seven days and seven nights without a word. Friends, this was the best moment of their ministry in the whole book of Job. Their trouble began on the eighth day, when they opened their mouths. They started to explain: Job, think about it, have you done something wrong? From chapter 38 God speaks in person, and at the end says that they had not spoken of Him what was right, as His servant Job had. Those who defended God were corrected by God. And the man who kept on protesting, God said, had spoken more rightly. Please keep this in your heart.

In 2011 the World Health Organization published a guide to psychological first aid, with World Vision among the bodies that produced it. Its reminders are plain: offer practical help, listen, and do not pressure people to tell their story. Hobfoll and other scholars identified five elements of support after disaster: safety, calm, a sense of efficacy, connection and hope. Of those five, safety is a very concrete matter: there must be water, a place to sleep, and knowledge of where one’s family is. If you go to a disaster zone and your first words are to ask whether the person believes in the Lord, it really is the wrong moment.
A few things please do not say anymore

I beg you, brothers and sisters, there are a few things please do not say to someone who has just lost a loved one. Do not say, “God wanted to take him home.” Do not say, “It is God’s good will.” Do not say, “That place worships idols, so this happened.” And there is one that many people think is in the Bible: “God will not give you more than you can bear.” First Corinthians 10 is about temptation, not earthquakes. So what should we say? We can say: I don’t know why. I’m here. Have you eaten today?
Paul used just one short sentence:
Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep. (Romans 12:15)
2. What we know and what we don’t

When it is time to talk, we should talk honestly. The Earth’s crust is divided into several plates that push against each other. The boundaries often stick, and pressure builds slowly. Press a plastic ruler down at the edge of a table and let it bend, and when your finger slips, it snaps back. A plate boundary is just like that, except that this ruler is hundreds of kilometers long and has been bending for hundreds of years.

Here is a fact that is hard to say. The same plate and volcanic activity that raises high mountains and takes part in the long-term carbon cycle is also related to our planet’s staying fit to live on over the long term. I say it because it is true. But please do not use this sentence to comfort anyone. You cannot say to a father searching the rubble for his child: but plates are very good for the climate. That sentence cannot answer “why him?”
It is not all nature’s doing

In 1755 the great Lisbon earthquake shook the whole intellectual world of Europe. Voltaire wrote a poem questioning God’s goodness. The next year Rousseau answered him with a letter and said something quite interesting; the gist of it was that it was not nature that built twenty thousand houses of six or seven stories close together.

More than two hundred years later, in 2011, two earthquake researchers wrote a commentary in Nature called “Corruption kills.” They analyzed the previous 30 years and found that about eighty-three percent of earthquake deaths from collapsing buildings occurred in countries with relatively high levels of corruption. The authors also explain that corruption is hard to quantify directly and is closely tied to poverty, so this is not a precise number. But the direction is very clear: for an earthquake of the same size, where you live and what kind of house you live in make an enormous difference. Please note that this is in no way blaming the dead. No one chooses to be born into poverty, and no one can inspect the steel bars inside the walls of their own apartment. It is a reminder to those with power, to those who build houses and those who inspect them, and that includes our own church buildings.
Spiritual meaning: do not pretend to have the answer

So what about God? Why does He allow it? Let me tell you honestly: Christians do not have one answer that everyone agrees on. Some say creation is broken; Paul says creation was subjected to vanity and groans together; the theologian Hart wrote a book after the South Asian tsunami opposing the idea that such disasters are a necessary part of God’s plan. But earthquakes are older than humankind, so how is that to be understood? The explanations differ a great deal. Some, like the physicist Polkinghorne, believe God gave creation real autonomy, and that a world able to form itself is better than a puppet theater; but is that enough for the victims? Others, like Carson, stress that both God’s sovereignty and His goodness must be held, admitting that the tension cannot be untied by humans; but that sentence is the easiest to say coldly.

My friends who do not believe will say: an all-powerful, all-good God should have made a world without tsunamis. That is a very serious question, it comes from a real conscience, and I do not intend to dispose of it from the pulpit in three sentences. All I can tell you is where I stand. I do not know the reason for that earthquake. But I know how Jesus answered a similar question, and I know where He Himself went.

In Luke 13, some people came to tell Jesus about a political massacre. Jesus Himself raised another matter, a tower that fell and killed eighteen people. Back then people thought the same way they do today: for something like this to happen, there must be something wrong with them. What did Jesus say?

Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them—do you think that they were worse offenders than all the men who dwell in Jerusalem? I tell you, no, but, unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way. (Luke 13:4-5)

No. The Lord Jesus said it with His own mouth. So from today on, brothers and sisters, wherever something happens, and whatever the people there believe, none of us is permitted to say in a group chat that this is retribution. Notice the second half, “unless you repent”: He is speaking to the living questioners. He draws back the finger that points at the dead and turns it toward everyone still standing, and toward me. In the same way, an earthquake is not a tool for calculating the date of the end; not even the angels know that day.
He wept, and He cried out

John 11: Lazarus has been dead four days. Jesus knew He was about to raise him, and by all logic He could have explained it clearly to Mary. What did He do? He asked, “Where have you laid him?” And then the Bible gives us the shortest sentence of all:

The One who had the answer chose to weep first. Then at Golgotha, He Himself cried out: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Brothers and sisters, the most painful question in the whole Bible was spoken from the mouth of the Son of God. So your question to God does not come before His. God did not mail us a disaster analysis report. He came in person, entered the deepest pain of humanity, died, and on the third day rose again. The cross does not answer every why, but it tells us that He is not watching from a distance.
Spiritual meaning: outstretched hands, and that Day

Church history has a testimony worth remembering. In the plague of the third century, a letter of Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria describes Christians visiting and caring for the sick, some of them dying as a result. Scholars caution that these are Christians’ own accounts and may overlook the good deeds of non-Christians. It is the same today. After 921, the Christian Salvation Service set up relief stations and supply depots, and many churches committed to long-term companionship; at the same time other religions and civic groups also rushed to the scene. This is not a competition, and we thank every pair of hands. We only ask that we ourselves not be absent. James asks very directly:

And if a brother or sister is naked and in lack of daily food, and one of you tells them, “Go in peace. Be warmed and filled;” yet you didn’t give them the things the body needs, what good is it? (James 2:15-16)

And our hope does not stop there. Paul says the whole creation groans and travails in pain together until now. It groans because it is waiting. One day, God will do something with His own hands that no relief agency can do:
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more. The first things have passed away.” (Revelation 21:4)

Brothers and sisters, today I have not given you a polished answer. I have only three reminders. First, sit down first: people matter more than tasks, and being with someone matters more than explaining. Second, never put a disaster on the account of its victims; Jesus said that with His own mouth. Third, roll up your sleeves: preparing for disasters and relief work are both loving our neighbor; Jesus is my example, He wept, and He also acted.

This week I ask you to do one thing: with your family or small group, confirm evacuation routes, an emergency kit or how to reach the elderly; choose a relief organization with transparent finances, or pray specifically for a disaster-stricken region. If you yourself have been through a disaster and often wake in the night or cannot get back to ordinary life, that is not a lack of faith. Please seek professional help, and tell someone you trust, so that we can walk with you.

Let us pray together: Lord, how long? We do not understand. Draw near to those who are still waiting for news, still cleaning up their homes, still waking in the night. Lord Jesus, You wept and You cried out; be with them. Forgive us for the careless words we have spoken. Make us outstretched hands. May the day when You wipe away every tear come soon. In Jesus’ name, amen.
